title: Development of RAFM steel for nuclear applications with reduced manganese, silicon and carbon content
abstract: In this work, we investigate an alternative route for the production of reduced activation ferritic-martensitic (RAFM) steels with reduced contents of manganese and carbon. Alternation of the chemical composition coupled with various heat treatments as well as quench & rolling procedures are applied in an attempt to reduce the DBTT without altering the nominal strength and ductility. The obtained experimental results on the mechanical properties and microstructural analysis are compared to the reference European RAFM steel i.e. Eurofer97. It is demonstrated that an alternation of the conventional heat treatment of the newly developed low Mn/C steel allows the production of a material with a ductile to brittle transition temperature as low as −133 °C and strength comparable to that of Eurofer97. On the other hand, the performed quench & rolling procedure does not lead to any noticeable reduction of the DBTT, albeit it significantly increases the tensile strength without compromising the ductility in the relevant operational temperature range.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: R&D programs on development of reduced activation ferritic martensitic (RAFM) steels started about 50 years ago and, initially, oriented on material design for fast reactors with the reduced swelling under high neutron fluxes  [1] . Along with the appearance of fusion-dedicated programs, RAFM steels became also attractive for the use as structural materials by designing nuclear fusion facilities. Hierarchical microstructure of martensite, consisting of packets, blocks, sub-blocks and laths, determines the high strength and toughness of RAFM steels as well as an increased resistance to volumetric swelling under neutron irradiation  [2] .

Reduced activation ferritic martensitic (RAFM) steels for fusion structural applications are under constant development in several labs worldwide  [3–7] . The closest application of the RAFM steels in nuclear fusion environment is the structural material for test blanket module for the tritium breeding in ITER. One of the concepts of tritium breeding modules (TBM) designs in ITER and DEMO projects foresees water as coolant media where its inlet temperature can be as low as 275 °C  [1,8] .

However, the sharp increase of the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) of the RAFM steels belongs to one of the undesirable scenarios by their use under conditions of fusion environment. According to scarce available data on high fluence neutron irradiation, the DBTT shift as well as the change of mechanical properties (reduction of the uniform and total elongation) depends strongly on irradiation dose and irradiation temperature  [9] . Under the irradiation temperature below 350 °C, the formation of dislocation loops, precipitates of α'-phase and solute-rich clusters leads to dislocation pinning, thus, suppressing the plastic deformation (i.e. causing embrittlement)  [10,11] . On the European fusion research roadmap, the attempt to develop so-called “low-temperature” RAFM (LT RAFM) steel grade was made aiming to support R&D works on the development of water cooled blanket concept  [12] . The baseline material for the fusion application is Eurofer97 RAFM steel (henceforth EU97) developed at KIT (Germany). Within that stream, one of the main issues to be addressed is the optimization of EU97-like steel grades with reduced DBTT and specially tailored microstructure and chemistry to suppress the accumulation of the irradiation damage in the relevant operational temperature range.

In this work, we present the results of the task dedicated to a development of so-called “clean” steel. The development is based on the EU97 composition, but the term “clean” is adopted since the contents of C, Mn and Si were severely reduced. The reason for the reduction of these elements comes in recent experimental findings by means of elemental chemical analysis using electron microscopy and atom probe tomography.

The evidences for the formation of the solute-rich clusters (induced by neutron irradiation) in RAFM steels have been presented about ten years ago, when advanced post-irradiation examination of model high-Cr alloys has been performed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atom probe tomography and small angle scattering  [13–15] . Thanks to a series of these works, it has been recognized that even at relatively low irradiation dose (0.5–1.5 dpa), the neutron irradiation at 300 °C causes the formation of high density (exceeding 10 23  m −3 ) of solute-rich clusters consisting of carbon, manganese and nickel/silicon, which provide significant contribution (up to 40%) to the total irradiation hardening. The formation of these clusters was tentatively assigned to the segregation at small dislocation loops  [16,17] , which might even be invisible to TEM due to the screening of the strain field by the segregated solutes. The first atom probe data on the neutron irradiated EU97 were obtained by Rogozhkin et al  [18] , where the material was irradiated up to 32 dpa at 332 °C in BOR60 fast reactor. In this work, the spatial correlation between manganese and silicon atoms forming fine-scale clusters with a density of up to 10 24  m −3  has been reported for the first time to take place in EU97 steel. At the same time, the atom probe study by Anderoglu et al.  [19]  performed on another 9Cr steel (HT9) irradiated in the fast flux test facility has also reported the formation of Mn-Si rich clusters formed around the donut-like objects, likely to be defined as dislocation loops. Very recently, the two studies performed in France  [20]  and USA  [21] , where EU97 was irradiated in BOR60, HFR (16 and 32 dpa at 332 °C) and HFIR (72 dpa in vicinity of 300 °C) reactors have also revealed the presence of segregation of different alloying elements including Mn and Si. Specifically, the work of Gomes-Ferrer et al.  [20]  highlights that the segregation of solutes (Si, P, Mn and sometimes Cr and Ni) has been observed at dislocation loops, dislocation lines, grain boundaries and sometimes forming clusters. The decorated objects are extensively surrounded by “Mn clouds”, around which a high density population of spherical CrMn-rich clusters which nucleate sometimes at the Cr-rich border of dislocation loops has been revealed. Hence, there is a number of independent studies performed in technological grades which clearly demonstrated that segregation of Mn, Ni, Si is found to correlate with the presence of dislocation loops or promote the solute-rich clusters as such.

Following the lessons of the above-given experimental review, it has been proposed to remove the elements contributing to the formation of the solute-rich clusters. Different parameters of thermal treatment (austenitization followed by tempering) were selected in order to optimize a combination of mechanical properties considering EU97 as a reference guideline. Additionally, in attempt to improve the strength (to compensate for the reduction of carbon) and DBTT, an intermediate cold-working step by quench & rolling was applied between the austenitization and tempering phases. The main hypothesis behind the impact of the cold rolling in the fabrication route was to achieve a refinement and redistribution of precipitates within grain matrix and grain boundaries. It should be noted that different technological processes (e.g., severe plastic deformation, equal channel angular pressing) were used in earlier studies aiming to obtain fine-grained microstructure in low-carbon steels using similar treatment  [22,23] .

As a reference material, EU97 steel grade with similar fabrication history and chemical composition was selected for the comparison of its properties with “clean” steel grades. The paper provides the information on nominal microstructure (metallographic analysis, scanning electron microscopy with electron back scatter diffraction analysis), impact Charpy testing, hardness and tensile properties as well as transmission electron microscopy applied on few pre-selected variants of the “clean” steels.

sections.heading: Fabrication history
paragraphs: The fabrication route of the studied steel grades started with the production of ingots, weighing about 60 kg and having a size of approx. 250 × 250 × 125 mm 3 . Subsequently, the lab-cast ingots were cut to rolling blocks of ± 70 mm thickness and rolled in several passes in temperature range of 1250–850 °C, with a reduction of 20–30 % per pass, to obtain the desired plate thickness (∼11 mm).

Table 1 
                          lists the parameters of the heat treatments which were used during the fabrication of the investigated steel grades. For clarity, the different heat treatments are marked as G.1.1 to G.1.5 which refer to Grade 1, i.e. the “clean” steel, whereas Grade 2 corresponds to the lab-cast EUROFER material  [24] .

An intermediate cold rolling operation with a reduction of 10 % was applied between the austenitization and tempering stage to increase the dislocation density in the material by cold working. The deformation is intended to minimize lath growth during tempering, potentially leading to a decrease in DBTT (see material G.1.5,  Table 1 ). As an additional effect, a more homogeneous distribution of fine precipitates is expected, by generating nucleation sites not only on the grain boundaries but also within the matrix.

sections.heading: Chemical composition
paragraphs:
Table 2 
                          represents the chemical compositions of a “clean” steel (=severe reduction of C and Mn) and two EUROFER-reference grades, i.e. EU97  [25]  and a “lab-cast” EUROFER fabricated by OCAS N.V.  [24] . It has to be noted that steel grades fabricated by OCAS, generally, have a lower silicon content compared to previously developed EU97.

sections.heading: Thermocalc assessment and thermal/thermomechanical treatment
paragraphs:
Thermocalc software, in combination with the thermodynamic database (Thermo Calc, “Thermo-Calc Documentation Set Version 2017a”, 2017 and Thermo Calc, “Thermo-Calc Software TCFE7, Steels/Fe-based Alloys Database”, 2013), was used to perform thermodynamic equilibrium calculations aiming to predict the formation of precipitates which might have a potential influence on the mechanical performance of material (e.g. toughness properties) as well as to predict the initiation and final temperatures of austenitic transformation α → ɤ ( A 1 
                          and  A 3 
                         , accordingly). By the evaluation of the mole fractions of iron allotropic phases and precipitates using Thermocalc, following phases were taken into consideration: ferrite α (bcc), austenite ɤ (fcc), M 23 C 6  and MX precipitates. Formation of Laves phase, (FeCr) 2 (Mo, W), was not foreseen since it only has a significant effect on mechanical behavior at temperatures higher than 600 °C which is above the upper operational temperature limit for water-cooled tritium breeder systems  [26] .

Proposed temperatures of austenitization were selected above A 3,  allowing full austenitic transformation (α → ɤ) and preventing undesired grain growth by selecting too high austenitization temperature. Performed estimations by Thermocalc revealed the temperature range of austenitic transformation for the “clean” steel (investigated material G.1.1 to G.1.5) to lie between 833 and 882 °C, thus, determining a lower temperature bound for further austenitization and an upper limit for tempering. The upper austenitization temperature was chosen to be 1050 °C based on the work of K. Chandravathi et al. who reported a drastic grain growth in RAFM steels when exceeding this temperature value  [27] .

Rendering information from the equilibrium precipitation state by using Thermocalc foresees the stability of carbon or nitrogen-based phases at a given temperature. Although the distribution and size of precipitates within the material cannot be predicted with thermodynamic equilibrium calculations ,  one could consider the proposed heat treatment as a balance between the contents of precipitates and the necessity of grain growth control. It is important to note that a decreased volume fraction of M 23 C 6  and MX precipitates is expected in the investigated grade, since the carbon content is significantly lower compared to EU97.

Estimated mole fractions of the composing phases at equilibrium for the temperature range 675–1050 °C are presented in  Table 3 
                         , reflecting the points of the applied heat treatment conditions. For materials G.1.1 to G.1.4, the concentration of M 23 C 6  phase is decreasing with temperature increase till its dissolution at 839 °C, while MX-type precipitates demonstrate slightly different behavior. The content of MX carbonitrides with predominantly V and N decreases till their complete dissolution at 1155 °C whereas MX carbonitrides with predominantly Ta and C are already fully dissolved at 1020 °C. Concentration of M 23 C 6  phase in Grade 2 is generally characterized by its higher content and higher dissolution temperature (∼893 °C) compared to Grade 1. In Grade 2, the MX carbonitrides with predominantly V and N have a lower concentration and MX carbonitrides with predominantly Ta and C exhibit higher content at 675–1050 °C. Accordingly, the selected austenitization temperature of 980 °C for G.1.4 is characterized by higher content of MX-type precipitates during austenitization comparing to G.1.1 to G.1.3 where the treatment temperature of 1020 °C is applied. Notable that, in the last case, the MX carbonitrides with predominantly Ta and C are completely dissolved during the austenitization according to the performed assessment with the use of Thermocalc (equilibrium condition).

sections.heading: LOM/EBSd
paragraphs: The microstructure of the model alloys was investigated by light optical microscopy (LOM) and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). The samples for LOM were polished to 1 µm and then etched with Vilella’s reagent (1 gr picric acid + 5 ml hydrochloric acid + 100 ml ethanol). Specimens for EBSD analysis were metallographically prepared up to a polishing step of 0.25 µm diamond paste. An additional polishing step for 15 min with a 35 nm colloidal silica suspension (OP-U) was performed afterwards to remove any residual deformation layer from the previous polishing steps. EBSD patterns were acquired on a JEOL JSM-6610LV equipped with a Bruker e-Flash HR detector. The orientation data were post-processed with EDAX-TSL OIM™ data analysis software. The measurements were performed with an acceleration voltage of 20 kV, working distance of 20 mm and tilt angle of 70° in a square grid. Step size was set to 0.38 µm.

Two clean-up procedures were applied to the raw data. Firstly, the neighbor confidence index (CI) of 0.1 was applied to reassign the points with CI lower than 0.1 to match the neighboring points with the highest CI. Secondly, a grain dilation threshold was used with a grain tolerance angle of 1° and minimum 5 pixels per grain.
Additionally, the prior austenite grains were reconstructed from EBSD scans with the help of ARPGE software.

sections.heading: TEM analysis
paragraphs: The samples were cut in slices of 10 by 3 by 0.5 mm using a Struers Accutom 50 cutting machine. The thickness of the slices was reduced by mechanical polishing on SiC paper of 500 grit size to approximately 0.3 mm. Afterwards, 3 mm discs were punched from the slices with a disc puncher. These discs were polished further on SiC paper with grit sizes of 1200 and 4000 to reduce the thickness to approximately 0.1 mm. The final step in the sample preparation is double jet electrochemical polishing on a Struers Tenupol-3 instrument. The electrolyte consisted of 25% sulfuric acid (H 2 SO 3 ) in 75% methanol (CH 3 OH) and polishing was performed at room temperature applying a voltage of 10 V until perforation. Two TEM samples from two chosen heats ( Table 1 , G.1.1 and G.1.4) were electropolished to obtain data from at least two different locations.

The samples were analyzed in a JEOL 3010 transmission electron microscope operating at 300 kV. Conventional diffraction contrast images and selected area diffraction patterns were recorded. The dislocation density (

A correction factor is applied for dislocations that are not visible as a result of extinction conditions. It was assumed that all dislocations are a/2 〈1 1 1〉 type dislocations, which occur most frequently in materials with a body centered cubic (bcc) crystal lattice like ferritic and martensitic steel.

The local composition of the bulk material or carbides was measured with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) with an Oxford Instruments Link INCA system installed on the microscope. Routines are available in the INCA software for the quantification of the EDS spectra, but the results need to be treated with care. A small Cu peak was measured in all spectra which is generated in Cu parts of the sample holder. Moreover, focusing the beam on the sample induces the deposit of carbon on the surface which will contribute to the spectrum. Therefore, the carbon content will always be over - estimated. Finally, it should be taken into account that when analyzing small particles, the interaction volume of the beam can be larger than the actual carbide. The chemical composition of the bulk material could therefore be incorporated in the EDS signal.

sections.heading: Microhardness tests
paragraphs: Vickers hardness (HV) measurements were carried out on Struers DuraScan 50 tester with a load of 49 N (5 kgf, HV5). Since HV measurements were performed right after the EBSD analysis, the specimen surface correspond to the condition provided in Section 3.1.1 of this work. Totally, 10 measurements per specimen were performed according to the ISO 6507 standard procedure.

sections.heading: Tensile tests
paragraphs: INSTRON Model 1362 test bench was used to perform tensile tests in the temperature range from room temperature (RT) to 400 °C, as this temperature range is the most critical in terms of irradiation–induced embrittlement. All tests were done at a strain rate of 6.3 × 10 -4  s −1 . Estimation of the YS and UTS values was the main aim of the performed tests according to the ASTM E8M standard. The tests were performed on cylindrical and flat tensile samples with the gauge cross section of 2.4 mm in diameter and 1.5 × 1.6 mm 2 , respectively.

sections.heading: Charpy tests
paragraphs: Experimental CEAST 15I set-up supplied with 15 J hammer was used to perform Charpy tests.

All tested specimens were cut from the plates with L-T orientation. The KLST type samples (27 × 4 × 3 mm 3 ) were used with the notch sharpened by a special tool to induce an acute cut (razor blade). Such a procedure ensures that the radius of the notch is 0.15 mm or lower. The preparation of the samples has been followed the recommendation provided by Lucon et al.  [28] . The preparation procedure applied in this study is identical to many other studies earlier performed by Chaouadi et al.  [29]  on reactor pressure vessel steels and by Lucon et al. on RAFM steels  [7] . Tests were performed following European standard ISO 148–1.

sections.heading: EBSD/LOm
paragraphs:
The optical micrographs of the investigated materials are given in  Fig. 1 
                            . All materials show a martensitic structure. The dimensions of the LOM-visible grains were comparable in all studied grades, given the resolution of the microscope. This is why EBSD inspection was applied to provide deeper details of the grain microstructure.

OIM analysis of EBSD data was used to quantify the equivalent circular block diameter (further denoted as a block size) of the investigated samples.  Fig. 2 
                             shows the grain maps of the five materials G.1.1 – G.1.5, as well as the lab - cast EU97. The martensitic blocks were determined as grains confined by HAGB, having a misorientation angle exceeding or equal to 15°. There is no significant difference in the block size (around 8 µm) or prior austenite grain (PAG) size (around 24 µm) for G.1.1 to G.1.4, which were austenitized at 980 and 1020 °C. Material G.1.5 has a slightly bigger PAG (around 33 µm) size and consequently a larger block size (around 10 µm) which is consistent with the higher austenitization temperature of 1050 °C.  Table 4 
                             summarizes the average block sizes, PAG sizes as well as measured hardness. All six samples were characterized on the RD-TD plane.

The choice of tempering temperature is determined by the necessity to recover material from the as-quenched condition (i.e., to decrease the density of structural defects) and to allow the precipitation to take place. Since tempering time of 90 min was used for all clean steels except G.1.5, the attention was focused on the analysis of temperature influence on tensile and impact properties of investigated grades.

It was observed that the increase of the tempering temperature (from 675 °C to 760 °C) was accompanied by nearly 50 % drop in hardness (HV5), in agreement with earlier observations based on EU97 grades  [3] . Similar results were obtained by studying the influence of tempering temperatures at fixed tempering time (60 min) on mechanical properties of T91 steel  [3] . In the same study, the toughness was found to increase by raising the annealing temperature, demonstrating a trade-off between the high strength and high toughness.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The results of the tensile mechanical tests applied on quenched & rolled grade (G.1.5) and lab-cast EU97 are presented in  Fig. 3 
                         . Material subjected to an intermediate operation of the cold rolling between austenitization and tempering (i.e. G.1.5) exhibits high values of YS and UTS which is illustrated in  Fig. 3 (a) as a setup of stress–strain curves and on  Fig. 3 (b) reporting the yield stress. To determine the tensile properties eight specimens per each grade were tested at RT, 200, 300 and 400 °C (two specimens per condition). The strength characteristics of the quench & rolled grade (G.1.5) were about 30% higher than that of the lab-cast EU97. The reported data on UTS, YS, reduced area, uniform and total elongations is also compared with the reference EU97 (batch 2) data  [30] .

Apparently, the applied tempering at 675 °C of G.1.5 does not lead to full recovery of the cold-worked material structure which should be characterized by a high density of defects (most likely dislocations). Notable that the quench & rolled material possesses only slightly lower strength values compared to high-dose neutron irradiated material. In particular, Klimenkov reported that neutron-irradiated EU97 samples (T irr  = 300 °C, dose ∼ 16.3 dpa) showed UTS values of about 880 MPa while measured concentration of defects was equaled to 4 × 10 21  cm −3  
                         [31] . Also, hardening effect was reported by J. Hoffmann et al. by implementing of the Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) into thermomechanical processing of EU97 steel, although, in this case, the increase of UTS and YS values was much smaller compared to the growth of mechanical characteristics which is observed in the current study  [32] . The occurrence of rather high yield stress of G.1.5 may explain rather low uniform elongation, see  Fig. 3 e, as the work hardening capacity of RAFM steels is limited. From this standpoint, the accumulation of the irradiation defects in this grade should lead to even faster reduction of the uniform elongation than in the reference E97.

Plastic deformation performance expressed as a total elongation of the investigated specimens is presented in  Fig. 3 f. Noteworthy, G.1.5 has lower ductility but, taking into account available experimental data of EU97 from the Materials Property Handbook, one can state that the ductility of G.1.5 lies below but close to the trend line established for previously developed and comprehensively investigated RAFM steel grades.

Fig. 4 
                          illustrates the results of Charpy tests systematically performed on all the investigated materials. Evidently, the increase of the tempering temperature leads to a shift of DBTT values towards lower temperatures. Materials G.1.3 and G.1.4 revealed lower transition temperatures compared to G.1.1 and G.1.2, tempered at 675 °C. Among all investigated steel materials, G.1.5 has the highest DBTT of about −75 °C, which was not expected since the cold rolling was expected to increase dislocation density and therefore was expected to reduce the DBTT. The results of static tensile tests have also shown that the reduction area and total elongation of this grade corresponds well to the data obtained in EU97 batch 2. A possible explanation for the relatively high DBTT value of G.1.5 could be the precipitate coarsening occurring exactly due to the presence of cold rolling deformation providing defects enabling enhanced atomic diffusion during the applied tempering stage. The investigation of the exact reason for this would require fabrication of several quenched & rolled materials and parametric study of tempering conditions followed by the parametric Charpy testing, which exceeds the boundaries of this study.

sections.heading: Transmission electron microscopy analysis
paragraphs: Given the assessment of the mechanical properties provided and given that the quench & rolling step did not result in the reduction of the DBTT, we have performed a detailed inspection of the microstructure of the two grades rendering the lowest (G.1.4) and highest DBTT (G.1.1) using TEM. The main purpose of the examination was to deliver information on lath size, dislocation microstructure and precipitate structure. For the sake of brevity and completeness, most of the TEM images are provided as on-line  supplementary material  while main images are embedded in the paper. All figures referred to as Fig.A* belong to the online  supplementary material .

sections.heading: Microstructure of G.1.4 – Low DBTT material
paragraphs:
A composite image of the grain structure of material G.1.4 is shown in  Fig. 5 
                            . It consists of a martensitic lath structure within the pre-austenitic grains as expected for the structure of EU97-type material. The laths are parallel over an area of several micrometers. Only in the top part of the image the orientation of the laths has changed. The average lath width of 350 nm was measured from areas of parallel laths. Dislocation lines were readily observed which appearance and density depend on the location. Examples of the line dislocations at two different locations in the material are shown in  Fig. A1  (see online  supplementary material ). Significant variations in line dislocation density occur, as for some lath grains like shown in  Fig. A1  (a) and (b), density varies between 1.5 and 6.7 × 10 14 /m 2 , leading to an average density of (4.0 ± 1.1) × 10 14 /m 2 .

Two different types of carbides were observed in this material. Three examples of the first type of carbide particles are shown in  Fig. 6 
                             and  Figs. A2 and A3  (see online  supplementary material ). These carbides are predominantly observed at the lath grain boundaries and at triple junctions. They have a roughly globular shape with some rounded and some faceted edges. Their size is of the order of a few hundred nanometers, ranging from 250 to 450 nm.

The crystal structure of the carbides is deduced from the diffraction patterns as presented in the figures. In all three cases a similar lattice can be recognized, but oriented along a different zone axis. The patterns agree with a face centered cubic lattice (fcc) with a lattice parameter of (10.9 ± 0.5) Å, which is oriented close to the 〈0 1 1〉 zone axis in  Fig. 6  and  Fig. A3  and close to the 〈1 1 2〉 axis in  Fig. A2  (see online  supplementary material ). This crystal structure agrees with the lattice of a M 23 C 6  type carbide.

The chemical composition of the carbides is measured in EDS spectra and the results are given in the respective figures. Because the carbides are a few hundred nanometers in size, the contribution from the bulk to the spectrum is insignificant. The carbon concentration, however, is overestimated and the quantification does not allow to determine the carbon to metal ratio. On a qualitative level, the EDS results are in very good agreement. The main element in the carbide is Cr (40–48 wt%) followed by iron (27–38 wt%). The W concentration in the carbide is 7.8 wt%, which is significantly higher than in the bulk. There is also a slight but well-resolvable enrichment by V yielding to 0.7–1.1 wt%. The obtained concentrations are also in good agreement with literature data on the composition of M 23 C 6  type carbides in Eurofer 97  [33] .

Examples of the second type of precipitates are shown in  Fig. 5  and  Fig. A4  (see online  supplementary material ). These precipitates are much smaller than the M 23 C 6  carbides and sizes range from a few nanometers up to 20 nm. They have a spherical shape and are distributed almost uniformly over the interior of the lath grains. Their number density is (5 ± 1) × 10 20 /m 3 , which is much higher compared to the density of M 23 C 6  carbides. The volume fraction is, however, limited to about 0.03% due to their small sizes.

The EDS spectra corresponding to these precipitates are given in  Fig. 7 
                             and  Fig. A4  (see online  supplementary material ). Because of their small sizes, it is certain that the bulk metal gives a large contribution to the spectrum. Additionally, the focusing of the beam generates a high carbon contamination. On a qualitative level, it can be concluded that the precipitate is enriched in Ta and to a smaller extend in V. The ratio of the Cr to Fe is comparable to the bulk, which indicates that these elements are not present in the precipitate at all. Based on this information, the carbide is identified as an MX type carbide and in particular as a (Ta,V)-C with varying Ta/V atomic ratios. The diffraction patterns of these precipitates contain insufficient information to identify the crystal structure. Usually, only one weak spot can be recognized. However, because the majority of the precipitates appear bright in the dark field images, one would expect that all these particles have the same crystal structure and the same orientation. A TaC type carbide has an fcc lattice with a lattice parameter of 4.456 Å. The few spots that were identified agree with a 〈1 1 1〉 or 〈2 0 0〉 plane of such a crystal structure.

sections.heading: Microstructure of G.1.1 – High DBTT material
paragraphs:
Compared to G.1.4, G.1.1 was austenitized at a higher temperature but tempered at a lower temperature. The grain structure of G.1.1 is given in  Fig. 8 
                             and is found to be very similar to G.1.4. Martensitic laths are formed within the pre-austenitic grains. Also, one can observe finer lath structure in G.1.1 than in G.1.4. The variation in grain size is greater in G.1.1 as lath width ranges from 100 up to several hundred nm, being 250 ± 50 nm on average. The pre-austenitic grain boundaries are clearly visible as they appear to be intensively decorated with carbides, which is expressed up to much lesser extend in G.1.4.

The line dislocation structure in the martensitic laths is shown in  Fig. A5  (see online  supplementary material ). The measured dislocation density varies from 4.4 up to 8.8 × 10 14 /m 2  giving an average density of (6.2 ± 0.9) × 10 14 /m 2 , which is slightly higher than in G.1.4.

The analysis of the carbides revealed a number of differences compared to G.1.4. The first type of carbide is shown in  Fig. 9 
                             and  Fig. A6  (see online  supplementary material ).  Fig. 7  (a) shows a prior-austenite grain boundary as recognized by the change in orientation of the martensitic laths. It is noted that this boundary is decorated with carbides. No such decoration was observed in G.1.4.

Fig. 9  (b) selects one of the grain boundary carbides and  Fig. 9  (c) shows the corresponding diffraction pattern. This pattern can be identified as an fcc lattice oriented close to a 〈1 1 0〉 zone axis and with a lattice parameter of 10.8 Å. This result is, within the precision of the measurement, the same as in  Fig. 6  and  Figs. A2 and A3  and in good agreement with the structure of a M 23 C 6  carbide. The chemical composition is determined from the EDS spectrum in  Fig. 9  (c). Also, this spectrum is in excellent agreement with the EDS spectra of the M 23 C 6  carbides in G.1.1. Similar kinds of carbides were also found at other locations in the sample and an example of such a carbide is given in  Fig. A6  (see online  supplementary material ). It was noted that twins were formed in this carbide similar to the ones in  Fig. A3  (see online  supplementary material ).

Even though only a small amount of carbides was measured, the carbides formed in G.1.1 are on average smaller than in G.1.4. The size of the carbides presented in  Fig. 9  (a) varies from 150 to 250 nm, although occasionally larger carbides (up to 450 nm) are observed as well, see  Fig. A6 .

The second type of precipitates is shown in  Fig. 10 
                            . These are small spherical or cubic particles with sizes that vary from a few nm up to 20 nm. The EDS spectrum, which suffers from a high C contamination and a significant contribution from the bulk, shows a strong Ta signal. This type of precipitates is again identified as MX precipitates, most likely TaC carbides, and the sizes are comparable to G.1.4. One difference is that the EDS spectrum shows a clear oxygen signal. It is likely that the TaC carbides in this sample took up some oxygen during the heat treatment. The number density of these carbides is again quite high and a density of 7.7 × 10 20 /m 3 , resulting still in a low volume fraction of about 0.04%.

* Fig. 10  (e) shows a detailed view of one of the TaC carbides. This carbide has a square shape in projection on the [0 0 1] plane which suggest a cubic shape in 3D. The white lines show the orientation of the [1 0 0], [1 1 0], [0 1 0] and  [1–10]  vectors, based on the diffraction pattern of  Fig. 8  (c). It can be observed that the edges of the carbide are parallel to the 〈1 0 0〉 vectors and that the side faces are parallel to the {1 0 0} planes of the steel.

The black arrows in  Fig. 8  (e) indicate a few tiny rod-shaped precipitates. The width of the rods is less than 1 nm and the length is only a few nanometers. The length axis is found to be parallel to a 〈1 0 0〉 direction. As the size of these defects is too small to give a detectable EDS signal or diffraction pattern, the nature of these precipitates is unclear.

In addition to the two above described precipitates, a third type of carbide was observed in G.1.1 that was not found in G.1.4. Two examples of this third type of carbide are shown in  Fig. 11 
                            . These carbides have a globular shape and a size of a few tens of nanometers, which is in between the size of the above discussed TaC and the M 23 C 6  carbides. The diffraction contrast images show that a high density of stacking faults is present in these carbides with a spacing of only a few atomic planes. This phenomenon gives extended streaking in the diffraction pattern and masks the crystallographic structure of the carbide. In the EDS spectrum, it is noted that these carbides are still strongly enriched in Cr, comparable to the M 23 C 6  carbides, but with reduced W signal.
Both the chemical composition and the high amount of stacking faults agree with a Cr 7 C 3  carbide  [34] .

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The implications obtained by the above-presented TEM analysis may be applied to rationalize the difference in the DBTT and hardness in G.1.1 and 1.4. First of all, the higher hardness of the G.1.1 (280 HV) could be explained by relatively high dislocation density (6 × 10 14  m −2 ), finer lath size (250 nm vs. 350 nm in G.1.4). The numerous decoration of the PAGs by carbides in G.1.1 is another feature that is not observed in G1.4. The presence of carbides along the PAG interfaces may stimulate the micro-crack coalescence and its growth along the PAG boundaries preventing crack arrest under dynamic impact load (i.e. Charpy test conditions). The density and mean size of small carbides are similar in G.1.1 and G.1.4. However, the presence of oxygen in the TaC particles is registered in G.1.1, which might mean some oxygen uptake during the heat treatment, which also be a reason for the reduced performance under dynamic impact testing conditions. Finally, the presence of the third type of carbide with a size of few tens of nanometers should also contribute to the higher value of hardness (and therefore higher DBTT) of G.1.1.

Prior to conclude, we would like to discuss the DBTT and hardness of the explored grades accounting for the information obtained by TEM. The DBTT and HV values of the studied grades and reference EU97-2 steel are provided in the diagram shown in  Fig. 12 
                      . The general trend to be read from this figure is that the higher the hardness – the higher the DBTT is.

Given the detailed TEM analysis, we have found that in high-DBTT grade (G1.1) the PAGs are numerously decorated by the carbides, contrary to the case of the microstructure of the lowest DBTT grade (G1.4). Another important observation made in the high-DBTT steel was the presence of small rod-shaped carbides and M 7 C 3  type carbides in addition to the M 23 C 6  and spherical MX carbides, which apparently contribute to the high value of HV. Note that dislocation density and lath size are nearly the same in G1.1 and G1.4, therefore the difference between the HV and DBTT values of these grades has to be attributed to the precipitate morphology and distribution.

Although tensile tests of G.1.1 to G.1.4 were not performed, one could expect, taking the measured micro-hardness results into consideration, that the strength of G.1.3 and G.1.4, lies in the same range as that of Grade 2 (lab cast Eurofer), which is slightly below the reference EU97 steel. Thus, the preliminary screening of the mechanical behavior of Mn/Si-reduced RAFM steels demonstrate a possibility to achieve the performance of EU97 given the appropriate heat treatment.

In this work, overall, we have made an attempt to develop a route for the fabrication of EU97-like RAFM steels with reduced content of carbon and manganese, driven by the assumption that it would enhance the resistance of the material against neutron irradiation damage in the low temperature range (i.e. 250–350 °C, where the neutron irradiation embrittlement associated with the hardening driven by dislocation loops formation and solute-rich clusters is known to limit the application resource). The chemical composition and heat treatment were designed based on thermodynamic calculations, which in particular led to the selection of rather low tempering temperature of 675 °C for some of the studied grades keeping in mind low temperature application as pointed above. In addition to the conventional heat treatment, an intermediate quench and rolling step was introduced aiming at improving strength and DBTT, simultaneously. The intermediate cold rolling step can be considered as an attractive method from the point of view of stabilization of microstructure for a long-term operation: a well-developed defect structure induced by rolling should retard the processes of atomic diffusion and the movement (climbing) of dislocations, overall resulting in a better creep and fatigue resistance. In addition to the quench and rolling, several dedicated thermal treatments were performed with an attempt to alter the precipitate distribution aiming at fine dispersion.

The application of the quench and rolling step yielded a considerable increase of the yield stress and UTS, as was expected, but at the same time led to a relatively high DBTT value, which was not expected. We explain this caveat by the coarsening of the precipitates, and presumably, by reduction of dislocation density which originates from the alternative heat treatment (wrt EU97) and overall decrease of the concentration of alloying elements in the solid solution (wrt EU97).

A detailed TEM analysis was performed for the clean steels with the highest and lowest DBTT values, given that SEM-EBSD and LOM analysis did not reveal any essential difference in the microstructure. The high-DBTT grade (G1.1) featured numerous decoration of PAGs by the carbides, contrary to the microstructure of the lowest DBTT grade (G1.4). Secondly, the presence of small rod-shaped carbides and M 7 C 3  type carbides in addition to the M 23 C 6  and spherical MX carbides was registered in the high-DBTT steel was, which explains a considerably higher hardness of G1.1.

Hence, we attribute a relatively high DBTT of the material G1.1 (compared to G1.4) to the differences in the carbide precipitation states, which could not have been predicted solely by the applied thermodynamics calculations. Important to emphasized that M 7 C 3  type carbides do not constitute an equilibrium phase in E97-type steels, and therefore the stability of and role played by these precipitates under irradiation and/or extended thermal ageing (keeping in mind low temperature range for applications) needs a dedicated study being out of the scope of this work.

Based on the measured microstructure, DBTT and hardness one can demonstrate that Mn/Si-reduced RAFM steel can reach the performance comparable to EU97-2 and lab-scale EU97 (Grade 2), given an appropriate heat treatment.

Investigation of the irradiation effects as well as high temperature mechanical testing are the next important steps required to demonstrate the potential of the material for the application in nuclear fusion/fission environment. The first neutron irradiation exposures have been performed and the subsequent high-resolution microscopy studies are ongoing  [35] .

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this work, an alternative heat treatment (G1.1 to 1.5) of which the conditions were designed by thermodynamic calculation was explored for a RAFM steel with reduced content of Mn, Si and C while baring comparable DBTT and strength with the baseline EU97 steel (G.2). Based on the presented results, microstructural analysis and discussion, the following conclusions can be drawn: 
                         
                            • 
                            In addition to the conventional heat treatment, an intermediate quench and rolling (G1.5) step was applied and they resulted in a considerable increase of the yield stress, but also in the undesirable increase of the DBTT. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            It is considered that the hardening of quenched steels is due the presence of small rod-shaped carbides and M7C3 type carbides in addition to the conventional M23C6 and spherical MX carbides. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            The relatively high DBTT of the material G1.1 (compared to G1.4) can be attributed to the differences in the carbide precipitation states. Important to emphasize that M7C3 type carbides do not constitute an equilibrium phase in E97-type steels. 
                         
                         
                            • 
                            Finally, it can be said that an appropriate DBTT and hardness are available for a Mn/Si reduced RAFM steel while keeping the performance comparable to EU97-2 and lab-scale EU97 (Grade 2) by choosing a specific heat treatment conditions with a lower normalization and tempering temperatures (G.1.4).
